output.title: What contact decay hides in a small business
output.body:
Contact decay is not usually a big strategy problem. In a 1-10 person business, it is the point where a lead, customer, or supplier contact goes stale and nobody notices until the opportunity has already slipped. You see it in a CRM, an inbox, or a spreadsheet that looks tidy right up until follow-up breaks down. The real issue is visibility. If you do not know which contacts have gone quiet, you cannot tell whether you have a sales problem, a process problem, or just a memory problem. Human memory is a brave little filing system, but it is not a system.

The practical next step is manual: take one week of your contact list and mark every record you already know has gone dormant. Then write down how you noticed each one. Was it a missed reply, an old quote, a customer who never came back, or a note you found too late? That gives you a clear boundary for automation. If your contacts already live in digital tools and the quiet ones are easy to spot once you look, a lightweight flag may be worth building. If most of them arrive by phone call or walk-in, AI may not be the right fit.

The point is not to automate everything. It is to see whether contact decay is hiding real work you keep doing by hand.
